title: In 1963 a man knocked through his basement wall and found a city for 20,000 people

cover.alt: A rock-cut passage in the Derinkuyu underground city, Cappadocia: rough carved walls, low arched openings and a lit tunnel leading deeper.

body: In 1963 a resident of Derinkuyu, in Cappadocia, Turkey, was renovating his house when he broke through a basement wall into a hidden room, and then into a network of tunnels. Cut into the rock, the underground city reaches about **85 m** deep and could shelter up to 20,000 people together with their livestock and food stores. Its first tunnels may have been dug by the Phrygians in the 8th–7th centuries BC; it was fully formed in Byzantine times and greatly enlarged during the Arab–Byzantine wars, roughly 780 to 1180. Huge rolling stone doors could seal it from the inside, each floor could be closed off separately, and a tunnel of 8–9 km links it to the underground city of Kaymaklı.

slides.question: How deep does Derinkuyu, the underground city in Cappadocia, Turkey, reach?
slides.explanation: About 85 m. A 55 m central shaft seems to have served as a well, and vertical shafts dividing into smaller vents carried air to the rooms.

slides.heading: Centuries of use, then centuries forgotten
slides.note: The city was greatly enlarged in the Arab–Byzantine wars; its earliest tunnels may be far older.

slides.question: What sealed the city against attackers?
slides.explanation: Large rolling stones closed the passages from the inside, and each floor could be shut off separately.

slides.heading: Who dug it?
slides.text: Nobody knows for sure who started it. The first rooms and tunnels may have been cut by the Phrygians in the 8th–7th centuries BC. The city reached its full form in Byzantine times and was greatly enlarged between about 780 and 1180, during the Arab–Byzantine wars. Stairs lead down to a church on the lowest level.
